items.title: Section: The Second Aspect Opens — A Fourfold Analysis of Arising Bodhicitta, Beginning With Its Cause

items.zh: 又即如是菩薩發心，略由四相應當了知。何等為四？一者、何相菩薩發心？二者、發心何所緣慮？三者、發心何狀、何相、何自性起？四者、發心有何勝利？由此四相，應當了知菩薩發心。謂諸菩薩勝解行住，已善積集一切善根，於菩薩行已正超出。略說是相菩薩發心。
items.en:
Furthermore, such a bodhisattva's own arising bodhicitta, in brief, has four marks that should be understood.
What are the four?
First, what mark does a bodhisattva's arising bodhicitta bear? Second, what object does arising bodhicitta take as its concern? Third, what state, what mark, and from what intrinsic nature does arising bodhicitta arise? Fourth, what benefit does arising bodhicitta bring? By these four marks, a bodhisattva's arising bodhicitta should be understood.
Namely, such bodhisattvas, at the abode of resolute practice, have already skilfully accumulated every wholesome root, and have already rightly gone beyond their former stage in bodhisattva practice. This, in brief, is the mark of a bodhisattva's arising bodhicitta.
Commentary: Regarding "every wholesome root" and the like — the Commentary on the Ten Grounds Sutra, in brief, distinguishes with ten phrases what body one relies upon to give rise to such a mind, namely this text's own "what mark does a bodhisattva's arising bodhicitta bear." That text places thickly accumulated wholesome roots first and manifesting great compassion last. Among the ten distinct phrases, the first phrase is the general statement, namely this text's own "already skilfully accumulated every wholesome root"; the remaining phrases are the particular statements, namely this text's own "already rightly gone beyond their former stage in bodhisattva practice." The words "gone beyond" mean being able to accomplish one's undertakings by simply according with one's own nature, unlike the abode of resolute practice, where only through repeated discriminating deliberation could one manage to cultivate and act at all.

items.title: Section: The Second Aspect — What Object Arising Bodhicitta Takes as Its Concern

items.zh: 又諸菩薩，緣當來世無倒速疾一切菩提資糧圓滿，一切菩薩利有情事圓滿，無上正等菩提一切種一切佛法圓滿，諸佛所作事業圓滿。略說緣慮如是發心。
items.en:
The second aspect: what object arising bodhicitta takes as concern. Furthermore, bodhisattvas take as their concern: the complete fulfilment, without error and swiftly, of every provision for awakening in the world to come; the complete fulfilment of every bodhisattva's own task of benefiting sentient beings; the complete fulfilment of unsurpassed, correct, complete awakening's every kind, every buddha-dharma; the complete fulfilment of the buddhas' own undertakings. In brief, it is by taking these as concern that bodhicitta arises in this way.
Commentary: Regarding "complete fulfilment of every kind, every buddha-dharma" — this speaks of the Tathāgata's own wondrous wisdom of every kind. Namely, being fully and equally awakened to whatever brings about a gathering of dharmas of benefit, a gathering of dharmas without benefit, and a gathering of dharmas neither of benefit nor without benefit. These three gatherings are called "every kind." All the dharmas contained within them, one should understand, are called every buddha-dharma.
Commentary: Regarding "complete fulfilment of the buddhas' own undertakings" — the Commentary on the Ten Grounds Sutra, in brief, distinguishes with ten phrases for what meaning such a mind arises, namely this text's own brief statement of taking these as concern, giving rise to bodhicitta in this way. That text places "in order to attain the buddhas' own wisdom" first, down to "in order to attain fearlessness in turning the great dharma-wheel" last. Within this, the buddhas' own wisdom means unsurpassed wisdom — knowing suffering, severing its origin, realising cessation, cultivating the path — and so this buddha-wisdom has nine distinct undertakings. Seeking this, such a mind arises, and so on at length. One should understand that the buddhas' own wisdom is exactly what was said before, the complete fulfilment of unsurpassed, correct, complete awakening's every kind, every buddha-dharma; the nine distinct undertakings are exactly what is said here, the complete fulfilment of the buddhas' own undertakings.

items.title: Section: The Third Aspect — the State, Mark, and Nature From Which Bodhicitta Arises

items.zh: 又諸菩薩，無倒速疾發起一切菩提資糧，隨順於諸有情一切菩薩所作，隨順獲得無上正等菩提無師自然妙智，隨順遍一切種諸佛所作事業，隨順廣大願心。
items.en:
The third aspect: the state, mark, and nature from which arising bodhicitta arises. Furthermore, bodhisattvas, without error and swiftly, give rise to every provision for awakening; according with sentient beings, they undertake every bodhisattva task; according with attaining unsurpassed, correct, complete awakening, they gain teacherless, spontaneous, wondrous wisdom; according with pervading every kind of the buddhas' own undertakings, they according with the vast, resolved mind.
Commentary: Regarding "without error and swiftly give rise to every provision for awakening" and the like — this explains the earlier question, what state, what mark, and from what intrinsic nature does arising bodhicitta arise. The Commentary on the Ten Grounds Sutra, in brief, distinguishes with ten phrases by what cause such a mind arises, namely what is displayed here. That text places great compassion first, down to "ultimate as empty space, to the very end of future time" last. From this one should understand: great compassion placed first is exactly the intrinsic nature from which arising bodhicitta arises; all the remaining phrases are its state and mark. That text's "wisdom's own heightened strength" is exactly this text's "without error and swiftly give rise to every provision for awakening." That text's "being subsumed within skilful means, a straightforward mind and profound mind both genuinely sincere, the Tathāgata's own immeasurable power, and the power of wisdom that well determines sentient beings" is exactly this text's "according with sentient beings, undertaking every bodhisattva task." That text's "according with spontaneous wisdom" is exactly this text's "according with attaining unsurpassed, correct, complete awakening's teacherless, spontaneous, wondrous wisdom." That text's "being able to receive all buddha-dharma, teaching and transforming through wisdom" is exactly this text's "according with pervading every kind of the buddhas' own undertakings." That text's "vast as the dharma-realm, ultimate as empty space, to the very end of future time" is exactly this text's "according with the vast, resolved mind."

items.title: Section: The Fourth Aspect Opens — Surpassing the Ordinary Bodhisattva Stage Through Eight Kinds of Transcendence

items.zh: 又諸菩薩發是心已，超過菩薩凡異生地，證入菩薩正性離生，生如來家，成佛真子，決定趣向正等菩提，決定紹繼如來聖種。
items.en:
The fourth aspect, benefit; first, surpassing the ordinary bodhisattva stage. Furthermore, bodhisattvas, having given rise to this mind, surpass the bodhisattva stage of an ordinary, unenlightened being, are certified into the bodhisattva's own true nature free of afflictive birth, are born into the Tathāgata's own family, become genuine children of the buddhas, are assured of proceeding towards correct, complete awakening, and are assured of carrying forward the Tathāgata's own noble lineage.
Commentary: Regarding "surpass the bodhisattva stage of an ordinary, unenlightened being" and the like — from here the treatise explains the earlier question, what benefit does arising bodhicitta bring. The Commentary on the Ten Grounds Sutra, in brief, distinguishes various marks of the moment such a mind arises, exactly what is displayed here. Surpassing the ordinary stage is the general statement, exactly this text's "surpass the bodhisattva stage of an ordinary, unenlightened being." Transcendence has eight kinds as particular statements, entering one's rank placed first, ultimate transcendence placed last. That text says: first, entering one's rank — first accomplishing a world-transcending mind, resembling first dwelling in the womb, as the sutra says, "entering the bodhisattva's own rank"; this is exactly "certified into the bodhisattva's own true nature free of afflictive birth." That text says: second, transcending one's family — resembling being born into a family, as the sutra says, "born into the buddhas' own family"; this is exactly "born into the Tathāgata's own family." That text says: third, transcending one's lineage — resembling a child arising from Mahāyāna practice, as the sutra says, "one's lineage now noble, beyond any reproach"; this is exactly "becoming a genuine child of the buddhas." That text says: fourth, transcending the path — because neither the worldly nor world-transcending path fully contains it, resembling being born onto a different path, as the sutra says, "passing beyond every worldly path, entering the world-transcending path"; this is exactly "assured of proceeding towards correct, complete awakening." That text says: eighth, ultimate transcendence — the buddha-lineage never severed, resembling the accomplishment of the ultimate path of nirvana, as the sutra says, "within the Tathāgata's own lineage, assured of ultimately reaching unsurpassed, correct, complete awakening"; this is exactly "assured of carrying forward the Tathāgata's own noble lineage." That text says: fifth, transcending the dharma-body; sixth, transcending one's sphere; seventh, transcending karmic action. Here, in brief, these are not explained in full.

items.title: Section: Abundant Joy Opens — Certified Purity, and Freedom From Anger, Harm, and Contention

items.zh: 又正獲得如實證淨，極多歡喜。於他有情遠離多分忿、害、鬪諍。
items.en:
Second, abundant joy; first, distinguishing six causes; first, genuinely attaining certified purity. Furthermore, genuinely attaining certified purity exactly as it is, one experiences abundant joy.
Commentary: Regarding "genuinely attaining certified purity exactly as it is" and the like — because faith in and reverence for the three jewels brings abundant joy, the Commentary on the Ten Grounds Sutra subsumes this within reverence-joy.
Second, freedom from anger. Towards other sentient beings, one is free of most resentment, harm, and contention.
Commentary: Regarding "free of most resentment, harm, and contention" — seeing sentient beings not practising as taught, or of improper conduct, and yet forbearing rather than growing angry, this is called freedom from resentment, subsumed in the Commentary on the Ten Grounds Sutra within non-anger-joy. Teaching and gathering in others with a compassion that is gentle and pliant is called freedom from harm, subsumed within non-affliction-joy. One's own mind subdued, remaining unperturbed while debating and explaining doctrine, is called freedom from contention, subsumed within non-corruption-joy. Saying "free of most" in this way is because the sutra says "mostly without resentment, mostly not afflicting sentient beings, mostly not corrupting others' meaning."

items.title: Section: Freedom From Arrogance, From Craving Joy, From Alarm — and the Sixfold Freedom From Fear Named

items.zh: 於一切種菩薩所作利眾生事，於一切種菩提資糧圓滿，於一切種無上菩提一切佛法，於一切種佛所作事，以淨增上意樂，攀緣勝解趣入。於是諸法速疾圓證。自觀己身能正隨順，如是解了，極多歡喜。又自觀見妙善廣大，能引出離，無染無等，攝受饒益身心歡喜，於此無量熾然善法皆悉成就。又自了知：我於無上正等菩提，今已隣近，於大菩提我勝意樂已得清淨，我今已離一切怖畏。由是因緣，極多歡喜。由諸菩薩已能發起善決定心，於五怖畏皆悉除斷。
items.en:
Third, freedom from arrogance. Towards every kind of bodhisattva undertaking that benefits sentient beings, every kind of complete fulfilment of awakening's provisions, every kind of buddha-dharma of unsurpassed awakening, and every kind of the buddhas' own undertaking, with a pure, heightened aspiration, one grasps and enters with resolute understanding. Swiftly and completely realising these dharmas, observing that one's own person genuinely accords correctly, understanding in this way, one experiences abundant joy.
Fourth, freedom from craving joy. Furthermore, observing for oneself the wondrously excellent vastness able to draw one out of attachment, undefiled and peerless, gathering in benefit for body and mind with joy, one accomplishes all these immeasurable, blazing wholesome dharmas.
Fifth, freedom from alarm. Furthermore, knowing for oneself: towards unsurpassed, correct, complete awakening, I am now near at hand; towards great awakening, my own excellent aspiration has already become pure; I am now free of every fear. By this cause, abundant joy arises.
Sixth, freedom from fear; first, naming them. Because such bodhisattvas have already given rise to a well-determined mind, the five fears are all entirely eliminated and severed.

items.title: Section: The Five Fears Explained One by One — Egolessness Removes Every Ground for Fear

items.zh: 由善修習無我妙智，分別我想尚不復轉，況當得有分別我愛、或資生愛。由是因緣，無不活畏。由於他所無所悕望，常自發起如是欲樂；我當饒益一切有情，非於有情有所求覓。由是因緣，無惡名畏。由離我見，於我無有失壞想轉，故無死畏。自知死後，於當來世決定值遇諸佛菩薩，由此決定無惡趣畏。由意樂見一切世間，尚無有一與我齊等，何況殊勝，是故無有處眾怯畏。
items.en:
Second, explaining; first, freedom from the fear of not surviving. Because one has thoroughly cultivated the wondrous wisdom of egolessness, the discriminating notion of "self" no longer even arises — much less arising any discrimination of what is loved as one's own, or attachment to life's necessities. By this cause, there is no fear of not surviving.
Second, freedom from the fear of ill repute. Because one has nothing to hope for from others, constantly arousing for oneself this very aspiration: I should bring benefit to every sentient being, not seeking anything at all from sentient beings in return. By this cause, there is no fear of ill repute.
Third, freedom from the fear of death. Because one has departed from the view of self, no notion of "self" being lost or destroyed arises. Therefore there is no fear of death.
Fourth, freedom from the fear of unfortunate rebirth. Knowing for oneself that after death, in the world to come, one will certainly encounter buddhas and bodhisattvas, by this certainty there is no fear of unfortunate rebirth.
Fifth, freedom from the fear of facing an assembly. Because, through one's own aspiration, one observes the entire world and finds not even a single being equal to oneself — let alone superior — therefore there is no timidity before any assembly.
Commentary: Regarding "through one's own aspiration, one observes the entire world" and the like — because one knows for oneself: towards great awakening, my own excellent aspiration has already become pure. One observes the entire world and finds none equal.

items.title: Section: The Summary Closes Abundant Joy — and With It, the Entire Fourfold Analysis of Arising Bodhicitta

items.zh: 菩薩如是遠離一切五種怖畏，遠離一切聞說甚深正法驚怖，遠離一切高慢憍傲，遠離一切他不饒益種種邪行所起瞋恚，遠離一切世財貪喜。無染污故，無所憎背；有熾然故，無俗意樂；能圓滿證一切善法。
items.en:
Second, the summary. Bodhisattvas, thus free of all five fears, are free of all terror at hearing the profound true dharma expounded, free of all arrogance and conceit, free of all resentment arising from others' harmful, distorted conduct, and free of all craving for worldly wealth. Undefiled, and so without aversion towards any being; blazing, and so without merely worldly intent; able to perfectly realise every wholesome dharma.
Commentary: Regarding "bodhisattvas, thus free of all five fears" and the like — this section, as appropriate, summarises what was said before. The five fears entirely eliminated and severed is exactly "free of all five fears." Genuinely certified pure towards great awakening, already free of every fear, is exactly "free of all terror at hearing the profound true dharma expounded." Correctly according with and understanding every kind is exactly "free of all arrogance and conceit." Free of resentment, harm, and contention towards other beings is exactly "free of all resentment arising from others' harmful, distorted conduct." Able to draw out of attachment, undefiled and peerless, gathering in benefit for body and mind with joy, is exactly "free of all craving for worldly wealth." Having thus summarised each point individually, the text then draws a total summary displaying the mark of arising joy — hence saying "undefiled" and "blazing" — by which one is able to perfectly realise every wholesome dharma. This summary of joy is here named a benefit.

items.title: Section: The Third Aspect Opens — Ten Great Vows Arising From the Purified, Excellent Aspiration

items.zh: 又現法中，能起菩薩一切精進，信增上力為前導故。於當來世，如前所說菩提分品十種大願，今即於此極歡喜住能具引發，由得清淨勝意樂故。為欲供養最勝有情真實福田大師法主，是故引發第一大願。
items.en:
Third aspect: giving rise to a correct vow; first, naming them. Furthermore, in the present life, led by the heightened power of faith as the forerunner, one is able to give rise to every kind of bodhisattva diligence. In the world to come, exactly as the chapter on the factors of awakening already explained, ten great vows — now, at this very abode of utmost joy, are able to be fully brought forth, because a purified, excellent aspiration has been attained.
Commentary: Regarding "in the world to come, exactly as the chapter on the factors of awakening already explained, ten great vows" — the chapter on the factors of awakening says: a bodhisattva's great vow should be understood as issuing from a correct vow. This again has ten kinds, explained at length (fascicle 45, page 3659 of the Nanjing edition). From that correct vow, one vows that in the future one will receive and gather every bodhisattva's wholesome dharma, and gather every kind of merit whatsoever. The ten great vows issue from that vow, and this is why it is said "in the world to come."
Second, explaining; first, distinguishing each mark individually; first, vows arising from specific matters; first, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha. In order to make offerings to the most excellent being among sentient beings, the genuine field of merit, the great teacher and lord of dharma, this is why the first great vow is given rise to.

items.title: Section: Vows Two Through Seven — Upholding the Dharma, Turning the Wheel, Right Conduct, Ripening Beings, Visiting Buddha-Lands, Purifying One's Own Field

items.zh: 為欲受持彼所宣說無上正法，是故引發第二大願。為欲勸請轉未曾有妙正法輪，是故引發第三大願。為欲順彼行菩薩行，是故引發第四大願。為欲成熟彼器有情，是故引發第五大願。為欲往趣諸佛國土，奉見如來，承事供養，聽受正法，是故引發第六大願。為淨修治自佛國土，是故引發第七大願。
items.en:
Second, for the sake of upholding the dharma. In order to uphold the unsurpassed true dharma proclaimed by the buddhas, this is why the second great vow is given rise to.
Third, for the sake of turning the dharma-wheel. In order to entreat the turning of the wondrous, unprecedented true dharma-wheel, this is why the third great vow is given rise to.
Fourth, for the sake of according with right conduct. In order to accord with and practice bodhisattva conduct, this is why the fourth great vow is given rise to.
Commentary: Regarding "in order to accord with and practice bodhisattva conduct" — the ten perfections are called bodhisattva conduct. This is what every bodhisattva should practise; in order to accord with this, the great vow is given rise to.
Fifth, for the sake of ripening sentient beings. In order to bring to maturity those sentient beings who are genuine vessels, this is why the fifth great vow is given rise to.
Commentary: Regarding "in order to bring to maturity those sentient beings who are genuine vessels" — the immeasurable realm of beings capable of being subdued is called the genuine vessel. Because being established in the lineage makes one capable of receiving the true dharma, this is the meaning of "vessel." Teaching the true dharma as appropriate to each, causing entry into the three kinds of awakening and ultimate liberation, is called maturation.
Sixth, for the sake of appearing everywhere. In order to journey to every buddha-land, behold the tathāgatas, attend upon and make offerings to them, and receive the true dharma, this is why the sixth great vow is given rise to.
Seventh, for the sake of purifying one's own field. In order to purify and cultivate one's own buddha-land, this is why the seventh great vow is given rise to.
Commentary: Regarding "in order to purify and cultivate one's own buddha-land" — the Commentary on the Ten Grounds Sutra says: purifying a buddha-land has seven aspects. First, identity-purity. Second, sovereignty-purity. Third, adornment-purity. Fourth, enjoyment-purity. Fifth, purity of the beings dwelling there. Sixth, cause-purity. Seventh, fruit-purity. This should be explained exactly as there.

blocks.text: At the first ground the bodhisattva is "born into the Tathāgata's family". Today: what that means, why the bodhisattva is full of joy, and why the five fears of Day 418 are gone.

Master Cháng Bǎi: "surpassing" means the first-ground bodhisattva can now spontaneously accomplish all bodhisattva qualities. Venerable Miào Jìng: only on reaching utmost joy is one truly beyond the ordinary.

Master Cháng Bǎi: at buddhahood no teacher's guidance is needed, hence "teacherless"; great compassion at the head is the nature of the first-ground arousal. Venerable Miào Jìng: the essence of arousing the mind is great compassion.

"Surpassing the ordinary bodhisattva stage, entering the true nature, born into the Tathāgata's family, becoming a true child of the buddhas." Master Cháng Bǎi: the Tathāgata's family is the dharma-nature, suchness. Venerable Miào Jìng: if you only study words without practising calm and insight, this phrase remains hazy.
Master Cháng Bǎi: resentment and harm are mental karma, fighting bodily, quarrelling verbal; "most" means not all: a small part remains.

"Hoping for nothing from others: I should benefit all beings, not seek anything from them." Venerable Miào Jìng: fear of ill repute comes from wanting something from others. And since there is no self at all, there is no thought of the self being destroyed; one never says "I'm ruined."
Venerable Miào Jìng: the faith here is the wisdom of prajñāpāramitā. Master Cháng Bǎi: the vows come from the aspiration already cultivated, hence "in future lives".
"To entreat the turning of the wondrous, unprecedented dharma-wheel." Master Cháng Bǎi: this is also called the vow of the eight phases.
The five fears and their cure fit together: fear of ill repute disappears when you want nothing from others; fear of ruin disappears when there is no self to be ruined.

quiz.q: The first mark of arising bodhicitta — "having correctly surpassed bodhisattva practice" — the English reads it as transcending the bodhisattva stage. How do the lectures read "surpassed"?
options: the first-ground bodhisattva can now accomplish everything spontaneously — only at utmost joy is one truly "beyond"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "surpassing" means the first-ground bodhisattva can now spontaneously accomplish all bodhisattva qualities. Venerable Miào Jìng: only on reaching utmost joy is one truly beyond — the English can be misread as leaving bodhisattva practice behind.

quiz.q: In "teacherless, spontaneous wondrous wisdom," how does Master Cháng Bǎi explain "teacherless," and what is the nature of arising bodhicitta?
options: at buddhahood no teacher is needed — realised oneself; great compassion at the head is the nature of this arising
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: at buddhahood no teacher's guidance is needed — one realises supreme wisdom oneself, hence "teacherless"; great compassion at the head is the nature of the first-ground arousal. Venerable Miào Jìng: the essence of arousing the mind is great compassion.

quiz.q: Having aroused this mind, what benefits does the bodhisattva gain?
options: surpassing the ordinary stage, entering the true nature free of birth, born into the Tathāgata's family, a true child, assured of awakening and of continuing the noble lineage
quiz.why: "Surpassing the ordinary bodhisattva stage, entering the true nature free of afflictive birth, born into the Tathāgata's family, becoming a true child of the buddhas, assured of awakening and of continuing the noble lineage." Venerable Miào Jìng: this bodhisattva's effort wasn't in vain.

quiz.q: How do the lectures explain "the Tathāgata's family"?
options: both: the family is the dharma-nature, suchness; Miào Jìng adds that without calm and insight, this phrase stays vague
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the Tathāgata's family is dharma-nature, suchness. Venerable Miào Jìng: the dharma-nature is the family; if you only study words without practising calm and insight, this phrase remains hazy.

quiz.q: "Free of most resentment, harm, and contention." How does Master Cháng Bǎi map these to the three karmas, and why "most"?
options: resentment and harm are mental, fighting bodily, quarreling verbal; "most" means not all — a little remains
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: resentment and harm are mental karma, fighting is bodily, quarreling verbal; "most" means not all — a small part remains incomplete. Venerable Miào Jìng: afflictions aren't fully gone — a little remains.

quiz.q: Why is there "no fear of ill repute"?
options: hoping for nothing from others — "I should benefit all beings, not seek from them"
quiz.why: "Hoping for nothing from others: I should benefit all beings, not seek anything from them." Venerable Miào Jìng: fear of ill repute comes from wanting something from others — then people talk.

quiz.q: On "no fear of death," what does Venerable Miào Jìng say?
options: there's no self at all, so no thought of a self destroyed — never "I'm finished"
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: there's no self at all, so no thought of the self being destroyed — one never says "I'm ruined." Master Cháng Bǎi agrees.

quiz.q: "In this life one arouses all diligence, led by the power of faith." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain this faith?
options: this faith is the wisdom of prajñāpāramitā
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: this faith is the wisdom of prajñāpāramitā. Master Cháng Bǎi: led by the power of pure faith, one arouses tireless diligence towards awakening.

quiz.q: The English links the ten vows to the "well-determined vow." Where do the lectures say they come from?
options: Cháng Bǎi: from the correct aspiration cultivated (factors-of-awakening chapter), hence "in future lives"; Miào Jìng: seeing ultimate truth clears afflictions — pure, excellent aspiration
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the ten great vows come from the correct aspiration already cultivated, hence "in future lives." Venerable Miào Jìng: seeing ultimate truth removes afflictions — pure, excellent aspiration. The English "well-determined vow" conflates this with the vow of §76–78.

quiz.q: What is the third great vow for?
options: to entreat the turning of the unprecedented dharma-wheel
quiz.why: "To entreat the turning of the wondrous, unprecedented dharma-wheel." Venerable Miào Jìng: requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel. Master Cháng Bǎi: also called the vow of the eight phases.
